entities.name: Jan Joosten van Lodensteijn
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jan Joosten van Lodensteijn (died 1623), known in Japan as Yayōsu (耶楊子), was a Dutch navigator and trader whose accidental arrival in Japan in 1600 profoundly shaped the nascent relationship between the emerging Dutch Republic and the unifying Japanese shogunate under Tokugawa Ieyasu. As one of the two surviving European officers from the ill-fated ship *De Liefde*, alongside the English pilot William Adams, Joosten became a crucial intermediary, offering invaluable insights into Western maritime technology and global trade networks to the burgeoning Tokugawa regime. His presence in Japan, spanning over two decades, helped lay the groundwork for the Dutch East India Company's (VOC) eventual exclusive trading rights at Dejima, thereby influencing Japan's foreign policy trajectory towards its long period of national seclusion.

Joosten's journey began in 1598 as a supercargo aboard *De Liefde*, part of a five-ship fleet dispatched by a Rotterdam merchant group to trade in the East Indies via the treacherous Strait of Magellan. After a calamitous two-year voyage that saw four ships lost and most of the crew perish, *De Liefde* limped into Usuki Bay, Bungo Province (modern-day Oita Prefecture), Kyushu, on April 19, 1600, with only 24 emaciated survivors. Interrogated by Tokugawa Ieyasu, the then-dominant daimyo, Joosten, along with William Adams, was spared execution and taken into Ieyasu's service. He was granted a residence in Edo (modern Tokyo) in a district that still bears his name (Yaesu), and a stipend, advising the shogun on shipbuilding, navigation, and international affairs. He participated in trading ventures and even attempted to return to the Netherlands multiple times, once in 1604, but was often prevented by Ieyasu, who valued his expertise.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Jan Joosten played a critical role in shaping early Dutch-Japanese relations, advising the Tokugawa shogunate on Western affairs and indirectly influencing Japan's foreign policy towards its two-century period of national seclusion (*sakoku*). His legacy is concretized by the Yaesu district in Tokyo, named after him.
